 The Dallas Mavericks are commemorating former head coach Don Nelson with a special tribute during their November 18, 2026, home game against the Golden State Warriors at American Airlines Center. The celebration, called Nellie Night, honors the late Basketball Hall of Famer, whose influence on both franchises included acquiring Dirk Nowitzki and Steve Nash in 1998.
 According to NBC Sports Bay Area, the first 10,000 ticketed fans attending Wednesday's game will receive a deck of playing cards inspired by Nelson. The giveaway reflects his enthusiasm for poker, a hobby that also led him to organize celebrity tournaments involving Willie Nelson, Woody Harrelson and Owen Wilson.

 Nelson died on August 9, 2026, in Frisco, Texas, at 86. He coached for a combined 19 seasons with Dallas and Golden State, including two separate tenures with the Warriors.
 Also Read

 His coaching career with Golden State began in 1988 after 11 seasons leading the Milwaukee Bucks. Nelson spent six complete seasons with the Warriors before resigning midway through his seventh season in 1995. Following one season with the New York Knicks, he joined Dallas in 1997 and coached there for seven full seasons before stepping down in 2005.
 Nelson returned to Golden State in 2006 and guided the Warriors to the playoffs in his first season. The eighth-seeded team defeated his former Dallas squad, which had finished first in the conference, in an upset that became associated with the We Believe Warriors.
 He retired in 2010 with 1,335 regular-season victories, the highest total in NBA history at that time. Gregg Popovich moved ahead of him in 2022, leaving Nelson second on the all-time coaching wins list.
 Also Read 
 Warriors Face Mavericks Without Stephen Curry in Dallas 
 According to Dallas Sports Journal, Nelson's influence extended beyond coaching. He also served as the Mavericks' general manager and orchestrated the transactions that brought Nowitzki and Nash to Dallas on June 24, 1998.
 Dallas initially held the sixth overall selection in the 1998 NBA Draft but arranged a deal with Milwaukee to move down to No. 9. The Mavericks received the draft rights to Nowitzki, selected ninth, and Pat Garrity, selected 19th. Milwaukee received the rights to Robert Traylor, whom Dallas had selected sixth.
 Nelson's international scouting operation played an important role in identifying Nowitzki. His son, Donnie Nelson, helped introduce the German prospect to the organization after working with the international team at the 1998 Nike Hoop Summit.

 Donnie arranged for the international players to practice at a Dallas YMCA, giving his father an opportunity to evaluate Nowitzki over an extended period. The young forward also spent a week living in Donnie's basement before the draft.
 Nelson described the organization's international scouting efforts during his account of the recruitment.
 "We scouted Europe more than anybody." Nelson said.

 The second transaction involved Nash, whom Phoenix had selected 15th overall in 1996. Dallas sent Garrity's draft rights, Martin Müürsepp, Bubba Wells and a 1999 first-round pick to the Suns in exchange for the Canadian point guard.
 Phoenix required the first-round selection to be unprotected, meaning the Suns would receive it regardless of Dallas' eventual position in the standings. The Mavericks finished with the ninth pick in the following draft, which Phoenix used to select Shawn Marion.
 Nelson had previously attempted to acquire Nash during the 1997-98 season but could not persuade Phoenix to complete a deal. Instead, Dallas acquired Cedric Ceballos from the Suns for Dennis Scott on February 18, 1998, according to Dallas Sports Journal.

 Nelson expressed satisfaction with the draft-night transactions in comments reported by The Dallas Morning News.
 "Things could not have gone better." Nelson said.
 Nowitzki and Nash arrived in Dallas on the same day and initially lived in the same apartment complex. Their partnership eventually became central to the Mavericks' development into a competitive NBA team.
 Also Read 
 Owen Beck Targets Full Time Role With Canadiens 
 Nowitzki's transition was initially challenging. The 1998-99 season was delayed by a lockout, and he did not sign his contract until shortly before the campaign began. He continued training in Germany with coach Holger Geschwindner during the extended preparation period.
 Nowitzki made his NBA debut on February 5, 1999, against Seattle in an overtime defeat. He missed all five field-goal attempts, converted two free throws and recorded four assists without a rebound in 16 minutes and 20 seconds.
 He finished his rookie season averaging 8.2 points and 3.4 rebounds across a campaign in which Dallas went 19-31. His three-point shooting percentage was 20.6%, but his development accelerated over the following seasons.
 By his third NBA season, Nowitzki averaged 21.8 points per game. His combination with Nash, particularly through pick-and-pop plays, helped Dallas win 53 games. Both players subsequently earned All-Star selections in the following season.
 Nelson's influence remained evident in the tributes following his death. During his August 13 celebration of life at Preston Hollow Presbyterian Church, Nash and Michael Finley delivered remarks. Nash also read a letter from Nowitzki, who was in Europe at the time.
 Nowitzki's message reflected on the confidence Nelson showed when selecting him in the 1998 draft.
 "You didn't just draft me. You believed in me." Nowitzki wrote.
 Nelson's November 18 tribute brings together the two franchises that defined much of his coaching career. The Mavericks and Warriors are scheduled to meet at American Airlines Center, with tipoff set for 7 p.m. Central Time.
